name: Naturally aspirated V12
description: Twelve cylinders in two banks, drawing air without a turbocharger or supercharger. A defining configuration for some of the most celebrated performance engines.
note: NA means naturally aspirated. Electric assistance does not change the combustion engine’s induction: the Revuelto combines an NA V12 with electric motors.

name: Twin-turbo V12
description: A V12 paired with two turbochargers. Exhaust energy drives the turbines, which power compressors that feed more air into the engine.
note: The 2024 Aston Martin Vanquish is an example of this configuration. It is a reference here, not a model in the current collection.

name: V12 engines
description: Twelve cylinders arranged in two banks of six around a common crankshaft. The V describes the arrangement, not how the engine is supplied with air.
note: A V12 can be naturally aspirated or turbocharged. Choose a signature combination above to explore one approach.

name: V10 engines
description: Ten cylinders arranged in two banks of five. This layout sits between the more familiar V8 and V12 in cylinder count.
note: The R8 performance in this collection uses a naturally aspirated V10. Cylinder count alone does not tell you an engine’s power.

name: V8 engines
description: Eight cylinders arranged in two banks of four. Different crankshafts, induction systems and tuning give V8 engines very different personalities.
note: The three V8 models in this collection use twin turbochargers. V8 engines are not inherently turbocharged.

name: V6 engines
description: Six cylinders arranged in two banks of three. A V6 and an inline-six have the same cylinder count, but a different physical layout.
note: The Ferrari 296 GTB’s twin-turbo V6 works with an electric motor. It is a reference example; the 296 is not in the current collection.

name: Flat-six engines
description: Six cylinders arranged in two horizontally opposed banks. The boxer configuration used by Porsche places its cylinders low in the car.
note: Flat describes the layout. It does not mean naturally aspirated: the GT3 here is NA, while other flat-six engines use turbocharging.

name: Inline-six engines
description: Six cylinders in a single straight row. Also called a straight-six, this architecture is distinct from a V6.
note: The M4 Competition in this collection uses a twin-turbo inline-six. BMW’s TwinPower Turbo branding does not change that layout.
source_name: BMW M · M3 and M4 engine details

name: Inline-four engines
description: Four cylinders in a single straight row. A widely used layout that can be naturally aspirated or fitted with forced induction.
note: Cylinder count is one part of the story. Capacity, boost, engine speed and tuning also shape its output and response.

name: W12 engines
description: Twelve cylinders in a compact W configuration. Despite sharing a cylinder count, it is a different architecture from a conventional V12.
note: The third-generation Continental GT Speed selected here uses a twin-turbo W12. Other Continental generations have different powertrains.

name: W16 engines
description: Sixteen cylinders in a W configuration. It is the cylinder architecture behind the original Bugatti Chiron’s combustion engine.
note: The Chiron in this collection pairs its W16 with four turbochargers. W16 names the layout; quad-turbo describes the induction.

name: Naturally aspirated engines
description: An engine that draws in air without a turbocharger or supercharger. Naturally aspirated engines can use many different cylinder layouts.
note: Explore the V12, V10 and flat-six examples below. A hybrid powertrain can still contain a naturally aspirated combustion engine.

name: Turbocharged engines
description: Exhaust gases spin a turbine connected to a compressor. The compressor increases the pressure of intake air before it enters the engine.
note: Single, twin and quad describe the number of turbochargers. The current collection includes twin-turbo and quad-turbo engines.

name: Supercharged engines
description: A compressor boosts the intake air, traditionally driven mechanically by the engine. A turbocharger instead takes its driving energy from exhaust gases.
note: Supercharging describes how air is supplied, not the cylinder layout. There are no supercharged models in this collection yet.
